div.head: This paper develops a generalized approach to schedulability analysis that is mathematically founded in a process algebra called RTSL. Within RTSL one may describe the functional behavior, timing behavior, timing constraints (or deadlines), and scheduling discipline for real-time systems. The formal semantics of RTSL then allows the reachable state space ofjnite state systems to be automatically generated and searched for timing exceptions. We provide a generalized schedulability analysis technique to perform this state-based analysis.
1: Introduction
div.p: A real-time system is one which has time constraints, normally called deadlines, the violation of which can lead to a degradation of system performance or complete failure. The problem of real-time schedulability analysis involves establishing that a set of concurrent processes will always meet its deadlines when executed under a particular scheduling discipline on a given system. In thls paper, we use techniques from process algebra [ 171 to define a general approach to real-time schedulability analysis that relies on the examination of the reachable state space of a system.

An approach to real-time schedulability analysis consists of three components: a process model, a scheduling discipline and a schedulability analysis algorithm. The process model specifies how the processes may act and interact, as well as the types of time constraints allowed. The scheduling discipline defines how the scheduler chooses among processes competing for processing time and other shared resources. Finally, the schedulability analysis algorithm may be used to determine whether a set of processes will meet its deadlines when executed under the given scheduling discipline.

earliest deadline scheduling (EDS) and least slack. In RMS, priorities are assigned to periodic processes on the basis of the period length with shorter periods implying higher priorities. RMS analysis techniques were given in [15,16] for independent processes and then extended to processes which share resources via priority inheritance protocols in [14, 21,22]. Limitations of existing RMS theory include an inability to handle direct synchronization between active processes and more than one time constraint per process. Except for the class of independent periodic processes, the EDS schedulability analysis algorithms typically consist of some form of exhaustive simulation to determine whether any execution sequence can result in a missed deadline [10,11,16,18,23]. The different process models allow various forms of inter-process communication; however, there are still limitations on these process interactions and the time constraints allowed.

An alternative form of analysis for real-time systems can be found in the field of formal specification and verification. In recent years, a number of formal models have been developed to reason about time in computer systems. Three major categories are Real-Time Logm [2], Timed AutomataA'ransition Systems [1, 2,12] and Timed Process Algebras [7,9,19]. In general, these formalisms represent attempts to extend existing formal computation theory to capture the notion of time and as such support richer process models than those considered in the scheduling literature.

However, a general limitation of existing formal methods intended for realtime (with the exception of [9]) is the lack of support for schedulability analysis. One problem is the common maximal parallelism assumption, which states that every process occupies its own processor, and therefore obviates the need for schedulability analysis [7]. Other models either do not support concurrency or do not consider the effects of specific scheduling disciplines [ 1, 2,12,19]. CCSR [9] represents a promising step in applying formal methods to real-time schedulability analysis. However, only fixed priority scheduling is considered and there are still limitations in the inter-process synchronization allowed.

In summary, various schedulability analysis approaches have been proposed; however, each model depends on a specific, and often limited, process model which is typically described informally. These informal descriptions can lead to difficulty in recognizing subtle differences between the models. Formal approaches for reasoning about timing properties of concurrent systems exist, but do not adequately address the concerns of schedulability analysis. These premises suggest that schedulability analysis technology can benefit from a formal examination using the techniques that have been developed for the formal speclfication and verification of programs.

In the rest of this paper, we present a generalized approach to schedulability analysis that has two components: a specification language (RTSL) and a reachability analysis algorithm. Once a system is specified, the operational semantics of RTSL formally defines the state space of the system. Timing information is encoded in the states of the system; thus one can determine whether any deadlines have been missed in a state. Reachability analysis can be performed on the state space to evaluate the schedulability of the system. If no states in which a deadline is missed are reachable, then the system is schedulable.

div.head: 2: A language for schedulability analysis
div.p: In general, a real-time system comprises a set of concurrently executing processes that are executed according to a given scheduling discipline. In this section, we define the syntax and formal semantics of Real-Time Specifcation Language (RTSL), which may be used to spec@ the processes and scheduling dlsciplines for uniprocessor real-time systems. The semantic account consists of two levels: the process level, which defines the state transitions that processes can engage in whtle in isolation, and the system level, which uses the processlevel semantics together with the scheduling discipline to characterize the transitions that a real-time system may engage in. The system semantics forms the basis for our reachability-based analysis approach, which is presented in Section 3.

The syntax of processes RTSL is built around the notion that programs take time to execute, and that real-time systems have constraints imposed on their execution times. To define RTSL, we first must spec^ a time domain D; in this paper we consider only discrete time and take D = N, the set of natural numbers. The discrete-time assumption asserts that all activity in a computer system progresses with dlscrete ticks of a global clock. We describe more detailed considerations for the discrete-time analysis of real-time computer systems and an analogous continuoustime model in [SI.

RTSL includes a component, Process Description Language (PDL), in which users may spec@ individual sequential processes. The syntax and semantics of PDL are based loosely on those of the process algebras CCS [17] and ACP [3]. In PDL, processes are built from actions using various process constructors; intuitively, actions may be thought of as the instructions that processes execute. PDL users may use three different kinds of actions in defining processes. Let L be a (countable) set of communication channels. In addition to the actions in APDL, RTSL includes actions of the form ~d , ad and Td, where d E D and a E L . These additional actions only appear in the semantics; users may not use them in the specification of their processes. We let ARTSL denote the set of all RTSL actions.
The syntax for PDL is given by the BNF grammar in The intuitive meaning of each of these constructs is as follows. PDL has two predefined processes nil and exc.

nil is the terminated process that can idle, but do no other action. The exception process, exc, identifies unsafe states in a process and cannot execute any action. X represents the name of a process variable. Process variables can be used in conjunction with the recursion operator, pX, to define processes with ongoing behavior. For example, pX.(a;x) is the process that can perform a actions ad infinitum. For convenience, we often write recursive definitions equationally; thus, we might use CLa;C to define a process C that behaves like pXa;X. A process a is capable of performing action a and terminating.

All other processes are built from these basic processes using the constructs shown in the PDL grammar. The basic process constructors are external choice (+), internal choice (@) and sequential composition (;), + and €B are used to represent nondeterministic branches in the execution of a process. The process a+b can start either a synchronization on action a or action b, depending on which complementary action is available.

+ is called an external choice operator because the branch selection is dependent upon the actions offered by other processes in the system. It is very similar to the operation of the Ada select statement. (33 is different from + in that the choice is made internally by the process. aCBb is able either to perform a or to perform b, but the environment cannot know whlch.

Code segments with nondeterministic execution times can be represented by using the choice operators + and 0. For example 2*tt9+210 is the process that does internal computation for 8 to 10 time units. Synchronizations with nondeterministic execution times can also be defined in this manner. Consider a send and receive of a message on channel b that takes either 2 or 3 time units to complete. We could represent these send and receive operations as F2+c3 and b+b3, respectively, with d@i) = d(Fi) = i. The sequential composition of processes P and Q (P;Q) behaves as P until P terminates and then behaves as Q. Thus, after the process (a+b);z4 completes either an a action or b action, it does 4 units of internal computation. Time constraints are specified for processes using the time constructs sw, fw and e. In sw(P,d), fw(P,d) and e(P,d) the d represents a deadline for the enclosed process. This deadline is measured relative to the time at which the enclosed process is first ready to execute. sw is the start within operator. sw(P,d) must perform the first action of P within d time units; otherwise, an exception is generated. fw is the finish within operator. fw(P,d) behaves as P as long as it finishes within d time units after it starts; otherwise, an exception is generated. e is the exactly operator. e is similar to fw except that e(P,d) takes exactly d time units to complete. If P finishes in d' time units where d' < d, then e(P,d) idles for d d ' time units. Note that although ~d (idle) actions do not appear explicitly in the PDL syntax, e can be used to define delay constructs as e(ni1,d) idles for exactly d time units. As long as an enclosed process meets the time constraint, sw and fw have no effect on its behavior. e, on the other hand, actually imposes timing behavior on the enclosed process.

If an exception is generated by one of the time constructs or by the exception process, the process is said to be in an exception state. An exception handler may be defined using the h operator. PhQ behaves as P as long as no exception occurs in P. If an exception occurs in P, then PhQ behaves as Q. If an exception occurs in a process that has no exception handler, then the process terminates in an exception state. The goal of our generalized approach to real-time schedulability analysis is to determine whether any un-handled exceptions are possible in a system of concurrently executing processes. If an un-handled exception is possible, then the system is not schedulable.
In addition to the processes definable in PDL, the full RTSL grammar includes the following auxiliary processes.

Named processes have the form Process-Name::P, where P is a process. Partially completed synchronization actions have the form ad and represent an action a after it has been started but has d units of processing time remaining. Synchronizing pairs are represented by terms of the form P(ad)Q, where P and Q are named processes. In P(ad)Q, processes P and Q are in the middle of a synchronization on action a, with d units of processing time required for the completion of the synchronization. Partially completed synchronization actions and synchronizing pairs may not be specified by a user, but may occur in the execution of a real-time system. Proc-is the set of all named and unnamed PDL processes. Proc includes the members of Proc together with partially completed synchronization actions and synchronizing pairs. Common types of real-time processes that RTSL can be used to spec@ include periodic, sporadic, and server. For example, a generic periodic process P with period t can be represented as pX.(e(P,t);X) or with the shorthand notation C %! e(P,t);C. Also, the sporadic process P with minimum interarrival time t can be defined as pX.(e(P,t);X 0 e(nil,l);X>, or P, %! e(P,t);P, @ e(nil,l);P,.

The basic synchronization primitive can be used to implement various forms of inter-process communication and cooperation. A binary semaphore S can be defined as S E p;v;S, where another process executes a p action to lock S and a V action to unlock S. The sw, fw and e operators allow the specification of time constraints for the completion of a whole process, as well as for subcomponents of a process.

Consider the process A fw(z3;sw(h, 4), 20). The whole process A must finish within 20 time units, but the T must start within 4 time units after the 3 units of internal computation (23) are completed.

div.head: 2.4.2: Basic priority inheritance protocol
div.p: The Basic Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP) is defined in [22] for processes that communicate only using shared critical sections. These restrictions on direct synchronization are needed to get the results that an a priori upper bound may be placed on the bloclung time that may be experienced by any process due to the use of shared resources.
Since our reachability analysis approach considers the dynamics of a real-time system, this result is not necessary and the restrictions may be removed.

The general idea behind priority inheritance is that if a hgher priority process PH becomes blocked by a lower priority process PL, then PL executes at PH's priority until PL finishes whatever it was doing that was blocking PH. In RTSL, a process may become blocked if it is ready to perform a synchronization action a, but no other process is ready to perform the complementary synchronization action T . To effect priority inheritance, there must be a way to determine the process that is the intended target for each synchronization. This is done with the .synchronization partner function. Definition 2.8: sp: Proc x 2hoc x Act+2hw is the synchronization partner function.

For any process P, the sort of P, written sort(P), is the set of all synchronization actions that may be performed by P or any of its derivatives (this definition of sort is similar to the one in [17]). sp(P,o,a) returns the set of all processes in the state o other than P that may execute the complementary action T either currently or at some later time. It is useful to note that in the tra&tional application of priority inheritance, the sp function is a constant function because active processes may only synchronize with server processes and server processes continually offer the same set of synchronization actions. Some general notes on the application of state-based analysis techniques are useful here. In the worst case, the problem commonly referred to as the stute explosion problem may arise: the number of system states can be exponential in the number of processes. However, we hypothesize that the filtering effects of scheduling disciplines and the regular structure of many real-time systems will tend to control the problem in practice. We plan to test this hypothesis experimentally as soon as an analysis tool based on RTSL has been developed. div.head: 4: Conclusions
div.p: This paper has developed a generalized approach to schedulability analysis that is mathematically founded in a process-algebra-based framework called RTSL. RTSL is used to describe the functional behavior, timing behavior, timing constraints (or deadlines), and scheduling discipline for real-time systems. Withm the framework of our approach, we can formally model the most commonly used real-time scheduling disciplines and provide a capability for modeling others. The formal semantics of RTSL uses the scheduling discipline as a parameter and allows the reachable state space of any system to be automatically generated and searched for timing exceptions.

The RTSL approach is less restrictive than existing real-time schedulability analysis approaches with respect to the kinds of processes and time constraints that can be specified and analyzed. The ability to spec@ more general types of processes provides greater flexibility to real-time system developers while maintaining the desired property of verifiability of schedulability. The modularity of the scheduling discipline in RTSL provides a common process model upon which various scheduling techniques may be tested. Finally, RTSL can serve as a theoretical foundation for developing and analyzing new and existing real-time scheduling approaches.

div.head: Future work includes plans to implement an analysis tool based on RTSL.
div.p: With such a tool we can further evaluate how the approach works for real systems. We also plan to extend RTSL for use with multiprocessor computer systems. Although this extension would be fairly simple for discrete time systems, the analysis of continuous time multiprocessor systems still presents many challenging problems. Another potentially fruitful area of research ,is the development of approximations to the reachability analysis described in this paper which are designed to reduce the complexity of the analysis. It may be possible, for example, to develop sdXcient conditions for the absence of exception states in a system that do not require the analysis of the global state space. Also in this area, we expect to be able to iden@ sub-classes of realtime systems for which the complexity of the analysis can be sigmficantly reduced. Such a class of systems is one for which only upper-bounds on execution time are necessary for analysis. Finally, we believe RTSL can serve as the formal basis for the development of a real- time programming language withm which the schedulability of the systems is verifiable.

div.head: 3: Reachability-based schedulability analysis of real-time systems
div.p: In this section, we characterize schedulability analysis as reachability analysis on the state space of a real-time system and give an example to illustrate the application of the RTSL approach to a simple real-time system. Using the system-level semantics, the behavior of any real-time system can be alternatively described by a state machine we call a timed transition system. This definition of a TTS is based on the labeled transition system from [6]. Although the timed transition system from [12] bears the same name as our TTS, there is no intended similarity. In the TTS for an RTSL system (PJI), each state is a set of processes, the start state is the set P, and transitions are as defined by the systemlevel operational semantics given in Figure 2.6.
